title: Alexander Skarsgård perfects the art of the going-out top | CNN
text:
EDITOR’S NOTE:Featuring the good, the bad and the ugly,‘Look of the Week’is a regular series dedicated to unpacking the most talked about outfit of the last seven days.

It has been hard to miss Alexander Skarsgård lately. The “Wicker” actor has had a winning streak of playful red carpet and press looks that have all been lessons in how tocheekily honor his co-star,be baby, or wear afreaky little shoe.

On Sunday at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles, his fashion instruction continued with a course on how to style the perfect going-out top. Wearing a layered head-to-toe look from Tom Ford by Haider Ackermann, the ensemble included a shimmering low-cut shirt and crystal-embroidered waistcoat beneath a black wool double-breasted jacket with a black orchid motif.

The going-out top was a millennial style staple throughout the 2000s. Any sequined, zippered or otherwise embellished tank or halter that could be paired with pants or a skirt and worn out for happy hour or a late night out fit the criteria. (For reference, please seeany paparazzi photo of Paris Hilton or Nicole Richieat the time.) Bonus points if it could be worn underneath a blazer for the day-to-night transition from the office to the club.

While the going-out top had a long dormant period as Gen Z began dressing down to go out — or not going to the club at all — it has beenmaking a steady comeback.Skarsgård is carrying the torch with a look fitting for six vodka sodas on a weeknight before triumphantly making it back into work the next morning. It’s both dapper and elegant, true to the sex appeal of Tom Ford, and is actually one of his more subtle options when compared to say,the time he wore no pants at all.

The stylist behind the Tom Ford look is Harry Lambert, who has also worked with Harry Styles, Jacob Elordi and Josh O’Connor — male stars who have all embraced a more expansive and delightful sense of masculinity in the ways that they dress. Since he began collaborating with Skarsgård, Lambert has often played up his 6’4” frame, subverting his proportions with gigantic thigh high boots, muscle-bearing halter tops, or itty-bitty short shorts. After all, why can’t a man built like a Viking have a bit of fun with what he wears? They’ve had plenty to work with based on the actors’ endless, eclectic roles, from the leather-daddy romance “Pillion” to the basket-weaving erotica “Wicker,” which launched a thousand think pieces on the uh, logistics of having a rattan-woven man as one’s lover.

Since his breakout role in the vampiric love triangle “True Blood,” the actor was fated to become a sex symbol, though he’s done so with unconventional roles and a fearless sense of style to match. His willingness to poke fun at his masculinity is part of the charm.

Menswear has been having a renaissance as many male celebrities have been keen to park the plain, stuffy suits and embrace styling that for too long, has only been considered feminine. After all, what’s more appealing than someone who is confident enough in who they are, and isn’t bound by gendered dress codes? Skarsgård may be one of Hollywood’s top male leads, but he’s also quite all right with being one of the girls.
